newsitem.title: FRANCE: Boeing merger seen speeding up Airbus changes.
newsitem.headline: Boeing merger seen speeding up Airbus changes.

text.p: The European Commission decision on Wednesday to give preliminary approval to the merger between U.S. aerospace giant Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp could be a blessing in disguise for Europe's Airbus, analysts said.
The merger, decided by the two companies in just 15 days after McDonnell lost an important contract, could convince the European Airbus partners to speed up their own merger, they added.

The European Union commission gave its green light on Wednesday, removing the last obstacle to the $15 billion aerospace merger, after Boeing in last-minute talks dropped its intention to conclude exclusive contracts with airlines.

"There was a broad agreement (within the Commission). The remedies the Commission was striving for have largely been supplied," Competition Commissioner Karel van Miert told a news conference in Brussels. A final decision will be made next week.
German Foreign Affairs Minister Klaus Kinkel said earlier in the day that Europe must focus on strengthening Airbus in response to the merger.

In France, European Affairs minister Pierre Moscovici said before the decision was announced that the Boeing concessions were "incomplete". After a weekly cabinet meeting President Jacques Chirac and Prime Minister Lionel Jospin urged the Commission to be firm.
The French aerospace industry, Airbus, Aerospatiale and enginemaker SNECMA, is a key sector of the economy.

"The exclusive contracts were the big worry to me," said an aerospace analyst at a Paris brokerage. "With the exclusive supply contracts Airbus would have virtually been kept off the U.S. market. Now they stand to win orders there, as they have shown in the past they can," he added.
Boeing dropped its intention to have exclusive supply contracts with U.S. airlines AMR Corp's American Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines .
Another analyst said that by giving up on what was an "outrageous" contract, Boeing had not really made a concession to the European Union.
In 1996, Boeing obtained 66 percent of new aircraft orders, McDonnell four percent and Airbus 30 percent.
"McDonnell was not a real competitor. It had effectively already dropped from the market," an analyst said.
He said that because airlines would prefer to keep a balance between the two suppliers, the balance of power would "almost mechanically" switch from the current 65/35 to 55/45 in favour of Boeing.

Airbus will have to do two things to secure its future in the ultra-competitive airline market where orders are picking up this year after about five meagre years -- become a real company and secure financing for its A-3XX project.

Toulouse-based Airbus Industrie (AIN1) is a consortium made up of French state-owned Ste Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain.
Aerospatiale and Deutsche Airbus have 38 percent each. British Aerospace Plc has 20 percent and CASA four percent.

The four companies and the governments of the member countries have agreed that Airbus should become a proper company with its own balance sheet and results. However the companies still disagree about which assets to transfer to Airbus, and at what price.

The A-3XX, a project which could cost up to $12 billion to develop, will be a very large plane which would also finally allow Airbus to cream away orders in a market segment where Boeing has a virtual monopoly with the 747.
Boeing has dropped its own plans to develop a very large plane, leaving the field for the moment to the Europeans

"Airbus needs to find the financing. I'm sure that the companies, BAe, DASA and Aerospatiale will chip in. Europe could also pay. But more is needed. There is talk that Lockheed Martin Corp could join and about alliances with Asian companies," an analyst said.
